newsitem.title: USA: Wiesenthal Center says Swiss banks' list overdue.
newsitem.headline: Wiesenthal Center says Swiss banks' list overdue.

text.p: The Nazi-hunting Simon Wiesenthal Center welcomed Tuesday's publication of a list of Holocaust victims who held Swiss bank accounts, but called it a "tiny step" that was half a century overdue.

"If there was any serious commitment to deal with the families who may have claims on the assets (in Swiss banks), why has nothing been done earlier?" asked Rabbi Abraham Cooper, associate dean of the Los Angeles-based Center.
"It calls into question why it was not done in '57, '67, or '87," Cooper told Reuters.

He was reacting to the unveiling in Zurich by Swiss banks of a list of pre-1945 account holders who may have perished in the Holocaust. The banks invited the victims' heirs to come forward to claim the assets.
Swiss banks published the unprecedented 2,000-name list in newspapers in 28 countries and on the Internet, breaking with a tradition of banking secrecy after criticism by Jewish groups.

Bankers who declined to be named said the total amount in dormant accounts opened by foreigners before the end of World War Two was around 60 million Swiss francs ($40.5 million), rather than about 43 million as the banks said last year.
Cooper was critical of the Swiss banks for the list released Tuesday.
"If the annoucement came a year ago it would have signaled to human rights organizations that maybe something had finally changed in the Swiss banks' thinking," he said.
"What was done today is a tiny step that is 40-50 years overdue. It is clear that finally, in some small measure, some Swiss banks had to answer publicly (what they had refused to do since the war)."

Cooper said the release of the account-holders' names was "a victory for the young generation" of people, media and government in Switzerland, rather than the Swiss banks who had made only "a symbolic gesture."

He noted that the Simon Wiesenthal Center had published its own list of some 1,500 Holocaust victims with accounts in Swiss banks. The list, posted on the Internet in February, had resulted in 17 families of victims coming forward, he said, and there had been more than 100,000 visits to the web page.
